lessons.title: The attacker's mindset & threat modeling
objectives: Think through a system from an attacker's perspective, not just a builder's
Explain how attacker's mindset changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect attacker's mindset with threat modeling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Secure systems aren't built by asking 'does this work' alone — they're built by also asking 'how could someone abuse this.' Threat modeling systematically walks through a system's entry points (login forms, file uploads, APIs) and asks what a malicious actor could do at each one, BEFORE it ships, rather than discovering it after a breach.
examples:
# threat modeling a login form:
# - what if someone submits 10,000 password guesses per second? (needs rate limiting)
# - what if someone submits a SQL query as the username? (needs input validation)
# - what if someone intercepts the request over an unencrypted connection? (needs HTTPS)
commonMistakes: Only testing that a feature works for legitimate, well-behaved input — security bugs live specifically in the malicious, unexpected, or malformed inputs a normal test plan never tries.
lessons.careerRelevance: Threat modeling is now a standard, expected step in real software design reviews, not an optional afterthought.

lessons.title: Authentication & authorization fundamentals
objectives: Distinguish authentication from authorization and identify common failures in each
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Explain how authentication vs authorization changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect authentication vs authorization with broken access control and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Authentication answers 'who are you' (login, verifying identity); authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do' (permissions, access control) — a system can correctly authenticate someone while still failing to properly check their authorization, letting a logged-in user access another user's data simply by changing an ID in a URL (a very common.
examples:
# authentication: verifying this request really comes from user #42 (login/session/token check)
# authorization: even though it's really user #42, are they ALLOWED to view order #999?
# -- a common bug: checking authentication but forgetting to check authorization at all
commonMistakes: Checking that a user is logged in but never verifying they own or have access to the SPECIFIC resource they're requesting — this exact gap is one of the most common real vulnerabilities in.
lessons.careerRelevance: Broken access control has topped real-world vulnerability prevalence rankings for years — this distinction is genuinely high-stakes, not academic. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Secure coding practices
objectives: Apply general secure-coding habits that prevent whole classes of vulnerabilities
Explain how input validation discipline changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect input validation discipline with least privilege and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A handful of habits prevent most common vulnerabilities at the source: validate and sanitize ALL external input (never trust it, as covered in the Backend and Prompt Engineering tracks), use parameterized queries always, apply least privilege to every credential and service account, never hardcode secrets in source code.
examples:
# never hardcode secrets:
# BAD:  api_key = "sk-abc123..."  (committed directly into source control)
# GOOD: api_key = os.environ["API_KEY"]  (loaded from environment/secret manager)
commonMistakes: Committing an API key or password directly into source control 'just for now' — once committed, it typically remains in git history even after being 'removed' in a later commit, unless.
lessons.careerRelevance: These habits are baseline expected practice in any real code review, not advanced or optional techniques.

lessons.title: Cryptography basics: hashing & encryption
objectives: Distinguish hashing from encryption and explain when each is used
Explain how hashing (one-way) changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect hashing (one-way) with encryption (two-way) and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Hashing is one-way: it turns data into a fixed-size fingerprint you can't reverse, used for password storage (you store the hash, never the real password, and check a login attempt by hashing it and comparing).
examples:
# password storage: HASH it (one-way) -- you never need the original password back,
# only to check if a new attempt matches: hash(attempt) == stored_hash

# sensitive data at rest (e.g. an SSN in a database): ENCRYPT it (two-way) --
# your application legitimately needs to decrypt and use the real value sometimes
commonMistakes: Storing passwords encrypted (reversibly) instead of hashed, or using a fast general-purpose hash (like plain MD5/SHA-256) instead of a slow, purpose-built password-hashing algorithm (like.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correct password storage is one of the most consequential, frequently-audited security decisions in any real system handling user accounts.

lessons.title: Network security fundamentals
objectives: Explain the basic mechanisms that protect data in transit and control network access
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: network segmentation, IDS/IPS awareness, TLS certificates / PKI.
Explain how TLS/HTTPS changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect TLS/HTTPS with firewalls & security groups and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: HTTPS (TLS) encrypts data in transit between a client and server, preventing eavesdropping and tampering on the network path — serving anything over plain HTTP today is a real, avoidable risk.
examples:
# without HTTPS: a login form submitted over plain HTTP sends the password
# in PLAIN TEXT across the network -- anyone on the same network path can read it
# with HTTPS: that same traffic is encrypted end-to-end between client and server
commonMistakes: Assuming an internal, 'private' network doesn't need encryption or access controls — internal networks are compromised in real breaches too; defense shouldn't rely on network location alone.
lessons.careerRelevance: Network security fundamentals connect directly to the Cloud Computing track's security-group lesson, applied specifically through a security lens. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Security testing & vulnerability scanning
objectives: Describe how real systems are tested for security vulnerabilities before and after shipping
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: vulnerability assessment / scanning.
Explain how dependency scanning changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect dependency scanning with static analysis and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Beyond normal functional testing, real systems undergo security-specific testing: automated dependency/vulnerability scanners check for known-vulnerable libraries, static analysis tools scan source code for common vulnerability patterns, and penetration testing has skilled testers actively try to break in, simulating a real attacker.
examples:
# a typical CI security pipeline step:
# dependency scanner flags 'library X v1.2 has a known critical vulnerability, upgrade to v1.3'
# -- caught automatically, before it ever reaches production
commonMistakes: Treating security testing as a one-time pre-launch checkbox rather than an ongoing practice — new vulnerabilities in dependencies are discovered constantly, after launch too, not just before.
lessons.careerRelevance: Automated security scanning in CI/CD pipelines is now standard practice at most companies with any real security maturity. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Incident response & security in the SDLC
objectives: Describe basic incident response steps and where security fits across the development lifecycle
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: incident evidence and log preservation.
Explain how incident response basics changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect incident response basics with security throughout the SDLC and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: When a security incident happens (a breach, a discovered vulnerability), a basic response follows: contain it (stop ongoing damage), assess scope (what was actually affected), remediate (fix the root cause, not just symptoms), and communicate transparently with affected users/stakeholders as required.
examples:
# security-in-SDLC, not security-as-an-afterthought:
# design: threat model this feature
# implement: secure coding practices, code review with security in mind
# test: automated scanning + targeted security test cases
# deploy: monitoring and alerting for anomalous activity
commonMistakes: Treating security as a final review step right before launch — 'shifting left' (considering security from the design phase onward) catches issues far more cheaply than finding them in.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding both incident response and SDLC-integrated security is what separates security-aware engineering from a reactive, checkbox-only approach. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: When a security incident happens (a breach, a discovered vulnerability), a basic response follows: contain it (stop ongoing damage), assess scope (what was actually affected), remediate (fix the root cause, not just symptoms), and communicate transparently with affected users/stakeholders as required.

# security-in-SDLC, not security-as-an-afterthought:
# design: threat model this feature
# implement: secure coding practices, code review with security in mind
# test: automated scanning + targeted security test cases

lessons.title: The CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability
objectives: Explain the three core security properties the CIA triad names
Explain how CIA triad changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect CIA triad with confidentiality and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The CIA triad names the three properties security work protects: Confidentiality (only authorized parties can view data), Integrity (data isn't modified without authorization, accidentally or maliciously), and Availability (systems and data remain accessible to legitimate users when needed).
examples:
# a stolen customer database = confidentiality breach
# a tampered financial record = integrity breach
# a DDoS attack taking a site offline = availability breach
# same triad, three very different kinds of harm
commonMistakes: Treating security as only about 'keeping data secret' (confidentiality) while overlooking integrity and availability, which are equally real security properties.
lessons.careerRelevance: The CIA triad is the most foundational, widely-shared vocabulary in all of security work.

lessons.title: OWASP Top 10 & CSRF
objectives: Recognize the OWASP Top 10 as a shared vocabulary, and understand CSRF
Explain how OWASP Top 10 changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect OWASP Top 10 with CSRF and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is a widely-referenced, regularly-updated list of the most critical web application security risks -- a shared vocabulary security teams and job postings alike use.
examples:
# CSRF example: a malicious page auto-submits a form to
# yourbank.com/transfer while you're still logged in there --
# your browser automatically attaches your session cookie
# Mitigation: CSRF tokens that a malicious third-party site can't know or forge
commonMistakes: Confusing CSRF with XSS -- CSRF exploits trust in the USER's authenticated session; XSS exploits trust in a SITE's ability to safely render content.
lessons.careerRelevance: Fluency with the OWASP Top 10's terminology is expected in almost any security-conscious engineering role.

quiz.q: Threat modeling is best done:
options: before a feature ships, during design
never, it's not worth the time

quiz.q: Cross-site scripting (XSS) typically results from:
options: rendering untrusted input as HTML/JavaScript without escaping

quiz.q: Authorization answers the question:
options: what are you allowed to do?

quiz.q: Passwords should generally be stored:
options: encrypted, so they can be decrypted later
hashed with a purpose-built password-hashing algorithm
in plain text for easy recovery

quiz.q: HTTPS/TLS primarily protects data:
options: in transit between client and server

quiz.q: What does the CIA triad stand for in security?
What does 'confidentiality' in the CIA triad protect against?
What does 'integrity' in the CIA triad protect against?
options: unauthorized or accidental modification of data

quiz.q: What does 'availability' in the CIA triad ensure?
options: systems and data remain accessible to authorized users when needed
only authorized users can view data

quiz.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: authentication verifies WHO you are; authorization determines WHAT you're allowed to do

quiz.q: Why hash passwords instead of encrypting them?
options: hashing and encryption are identical for this purpose
hashing is one-way, so even if the hash is stolen, the original password can't be directly recovered from it
encryption is always weaker than hashing
passwords should never be transformed at all

quiz.q: What does 'one-way' mean for a hash function?
options: it can be reversed with the right key
you can't feasibly reconstruct the original input from the hash output
it only works one time per password
it means the hash is always the same length as the input

quiz.q: Why is a slow, purpose-built hashing algorithm (like bcrypt) preferred for passwords over a fast general-purpose hash?
options: speed doesn't matter for password hashing
slowness deliberately makes brute-force password-guessing attacks much more expensive for an attacker
fast hashes are always more secure
bcrypt is faster, which is why it's preferred

quiz.q: What is the difference between hashing and encryption?
options: hashing is one-way and irreversible; encryption is two-way and can be decrypted with the right key

quiz.q: What is SQL injection?
options: an attack where untrusted input is inserted into a SQL query in a way that changes its intended logic

quiz.q: What is the standard defense against SQL injection?
options: parameterized queries/prepared statements, which separate query structure from user data

quiz.q: What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
options: injecting malicious script into a web page that then runs in other users' browsers

quiz.q: What is the standard defense against XSS?
options: properly escaping/encoding user-controlled content before rendering it in HTML

quiz.q: What does CSRF stand for?
How does a CSRF attack work?
options: it injects a malicious script into a page
it tricks a logged-in user's browser into submitting an unwanted request to a site they're authenticated on
it steals passwords directly from a database
it floods a server with traffic

quiz.q: What is a standard defense against CSRF?
options: using CSRF tokens that a malicious third-party site can't know or forge

quiz.q: What does the principle of least privilege mean?
options: giving every user maximum access for convenience
granting only the minimum access/permissions actually needed to perform a task
disabling all permissions by default with no exceptions

quiz.q: Why does least privilege reduce security risk?
options: limiting access limits the potential damage if an account or system is compromised
least privilege only matters for physical security
broader access is always more secure

quiz.q: What does the OWASP Top 10 represent?
options: a widely-referenced, regularly-updated list of the most critical web application security risks

quiz.q: What does TLS/HTTPS primarily provide?
options: encrypted communication between a client and server, protecting data in transit

quiz.q: What is broken access control?
options: a flaw where users can access resources or perform actions they shouldn't be authorized for
a type of encryption weakness only

quiz.q: Why check permissions on every request, not just at login?
options: checking once at login is always sufficient
a user's permissions or session validity can change, and per-request checks prevent using a stale or escalated authorization
per-request checks always slow down the system unacceptably
this only matters for banking applications

quiz.q: What does 'shift-left security' mean?
options: moving security responsibilities to a separate team entirely
addressing security considerations earlier in the development process, rather than only at the end

quiz.q: What is the purpose of dependency scanning?
options: identifying known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries/packages a project depends on

quiz.q: What is penetration testing?
options: authorized, simulated attacks against a system to find real exploitable vulnerabilities before attackers do
